items.text: I work remotely  for a HH & Hopsice agency in Michigan they just got approved  by Medicaid to submit claims do you know how I can contact them or where I can get a billing guide? What I'm  also needing is a payor ID.

topComments.text:
Yes, Medicaid billing can be a little confusing when an agency is newly approved. You’ll want to confirm the correct Michigan Medicaid billing manual, enrollment/EDI requirements, and the specific payer ID used by your clearinghouse for electronic claims.

If you need help finding the billing guide, payer ID, claim submission requirements, or setting up the billing workflow, feel free to DM me. I’d be happy to help point you in the right direction.
Please look at the contract packet that they received.

items.text: To my friends on Medicare!  Stay away from Devoted Medicare Advantage!  They will resend a hospital payment and YOU will be responsible for that amount out of pocket!  This will be on top of what you’ve already paid to the hospital for the contracted amount for the procedure!

topComments.text:
If you mean Devoted Medicare Advantage paid the hospital and then later took that payment back, that does not automatically mean the patient can legally be made responsible for the amount Devoted recouped.

For a contracted/in-network Medicare Advantage provider, CMS rules generally prohibit the provider from balance billing the member beyond the member’s plan-approved deductible, copay, or coinsurance. CMS specifically states that contracted MA providers cannot balance bill the enrollee. 

Devoted is allowed to conduct post-payment audits and recoup an overpayment from a provider when it determines a claim was paid incorrectly. Devoted confirms that it performs post-pay audits as part of its payment-integrity process.  But a recoupment between Devoted and the hospital does not, by itself, transfer that debt to the patient.

There are exceptions—for example, if the service ultimately is determined not covered, certain notice requirements were met, or the patient truly has additional responsibility under the plan. But the hospital generally cannot simply say, “Devoted took back $10,000, therefore you owe us $10,000.”

In fact, CMS strengthened Medicare Advantage protections for 2026, including rules around adverse coverage decisions and previously approved inpatient admissions. 

If you like you can send /DM me the exact wording from the Devoted EOB or the hospital notice—especially the denial/recoupment reason and whether it shows PR, CO, or another adjustment code—I can tell you whether that amount appears to be patient responsibility or hospital/Devoted responsibility. CMS explains that PR means patient responsibility, while CO means contractual/provider responsibility. I’ll explain it to you and help you understand.

I do this for a living and You need to fight this because. They cannot balance bill the pt because they recouped the payment from the hospital. The hospital probably messed up by not getting pre authorization or billed without having everything documented.

A clinician finishes a full day of patient visits, only to open their laptop late at night to tackle a mountain of unfinished charts, missing orders, and backlogged routine calls from their own bed or couch?

That’s what’s known as “pajama time” and it’s one of the leading causes of clinician burnout and high turnover.

Documentation backlogs and administrative prep shouldn’t follow your team home into their evenings and weekends. Delegating tasks like pre-chart gathering, order tracking, and follow-up calls directly protects your clinicians' energy, prevents exhaustion, and lets them fully disconnect after hours.

For home health agencies and healthcare practices, it’s not just about getting charts done, it’s about safeguarding your team’s well-being so they can deliver their best care and stay with your agency long-term.

The question is: Is your agency protecting your clinicians' personal time, or is admin work following them home?

items.text: Also…… MAC! I was not aware we had an MAC to help with looking up previously submitted NOA’s. How do I set this up? Feeling silly for not knowing.

topComments.text:
Don’t feel silly—this can be confusing when you’re new to the process. Your MAC’s online portal can generally be used to check claim/NOA information and other beneficiary details, depending on the access you have.

For Palmetto GBA, I’d start by making sure your agency has the appropriate portal access and user permissions. Once set up, you can use the portal to check previously submitted NOAs instead of relying only on phone calls.

If you need help with the setup or navigating the NOA/HH billing process, feel free to DM me. Happy to help!

Go to your Mac’s website and register for an account 
Yes you will be able up view NOA and claim status

items.text:
Question….
Say you admit a patient to home health 9/18/26. 

Then on 9/19/26 another company files an NOA for home health for that patient.

The patient requested our home health which was the 9/18/26 SOC . 

Palmetto says the NOA submitted by the other company is still active. They said they would retract it. But that could take days. 

We have to send our NOA today. It’s day 5. 

I was instructed by Palmetto to just submit it with condition code 47. With transfer date of 9/18/26. 
This is confusing to me considering they did a SOC on 9/19/26. 

What are your thoughts?

topComments.text:
The soc is for your agency’s start /admit date 
That is what you are reporting on an NOA with the code 47. Do as they say, get the NOA approved and then bill in 30 days. Your Medicare MAC will tell you what to do to correct things. You can always call them back for clarification and peace of mind.
It’s an automation issue - do CC 47 but keep the dates your own. Because the system already has the other NOA, you need to request the override (even though you were a day earlier).
